1) Step-by-step roadmap (clinical / research workflow)
	1.	Patient selection & counselling
	•	Choose candidates (often people with HIV who also need a hematologic transplant, or volunteers in tightly controlled trials). Extensive informed consent and counselling are essential because of risks.  ￼
	2.	Baseline reservoir and immune mapping
	•	Measure HIV reservoir size and location (blood, lymph nodes, gut, CSF), CD4 counts, HLA typing, and general health to plan strategies. Reservoir mapping guides how aggressive the follow-up clearance steps must be.  ￼
	3.	Harvest patient’s hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) or obtain donor HSCs
	•	Collect CD34+ stem/progenitor cells from bone marrow or mobilized peripheral blood (or identify matched donor with CCR5Δ32 if available).  ￼
	4.	Ex vivo gene engineering of HSCs
	•	Edit CCR5 (e.g., CRISPR/Cas9, ZFN) to knock out or disrupt the CCR5 gene so descendant immune cells lack CCR5 and are largely resistant to CCR5-tropic HIV. Alternative edits can add protective transgenes (e.g., antiviral factors) or suicide switches. Early trials show feasibility.  ￼
	5.	Extensive QC and safety testing of edited cells
	•	Check editing efficiency, off-target edits, clonality, replication competence, and sterility. Only cells that pass safety checks are used.  ￼
	6.	Conditioning regimen (myeloablation or reduced intensity)
	•	Patient receives chemotherapy +/- radiation to make space in the bone marrow for the edited cells. Intensity affects graft success and risk.  ￼
	7.	Transplant infusion of edited HSCs
	•	Infuse the engineered stem cells; they engraft, differentiate, and over weeks–months repopulate the immune system with resistant cells.  ￼
	8.	Supportive care and control of graft complications
	•	Monitor for graft-versus-host disease (GvHD) (in allogeneic transplants), infections, cytopenias; provide antimicrobials, transfusions, and immunosuppression if needed.  ￼
	9.	Optional/parallel reservoir-reduction steps
	•	Combine with strategies to reduce existing reservoirs before or after transplant: immune effectors (CAR-T, bnAbs), latency reversing agents to expose latent cells, or graft-versus-reservoir effects from donor cells. These improve chances of eliminating residual HIV.  ￼
	10.	Analytical Treatment Interruption (ATI) under watchful monitoring

	•	If ART has been continued throughout, researchers may pause ART (ATI) to test whether HIV rebounds. Close virologic and clinical monitoring is required. Some transplant recipients have remained in remission after ATI.  ￼

	11.	Long-term follow up

	•	Monitor immune function, reservoir assays, and late complications (secondary cancers, chronic GvHD, long-term off-target effects). Durable remission may be declared only after years of undetectable virus off ART.  ￼

⸻

2) Main scientific & safety challenges (why it’s hard)
	•	Incomplete editing / mosaic reconstitution: not every HSC will be edited; residual susceptible cells can let HIV re-establish. High editing efficiency in true long-lived HSCs is critical.  ￼
	•	Viral escape (CXCR4 tropism): many HIV variants use CXCR4 instead of CCR5. Knocking out CCR5 protects only against CCR5-tropic viruses — other strains could still infect. Multiple safeguards or multi-target strategies are needed.  ￼
	•	Latent reservoirs outside blood: infected cells in brain, lymph nodes, gut and other tissues can persist even after blood is repopulated; they must be cleared or permanently silenced. That’s why peripheral replacement alone may not cure without reservoir-targeting interventions.  ￼
	•	Risks of conditioning and transplantation: the chemo/radiation required to allow engraftment is toxic and can be life-threatening; graft-versus-host disease is a major risk in allogeneic transplants. That is why transplants are currently reserved for people who need them for other diseases (e.g., leukemia).  ￼
	•	Off-target editing safety & regulatory hurdles: CRISPR/ZFN carries potential off-target cuts or chromosomal rearrangements. Regulators require long follow-up and stringent safety data. Early trials show feasibility but cautious monitoring continues.  ￼

⸻

3) Complementary or alternative strategies (often used together)
	•	CAR-T cells or engineered CD8 T cells: to find and kill infected cells; useful to clear residual reservoirs and are already in early human trials.  ￼
	•	Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) and bispecifics: help tag infected cells and reduce reservoir.  ￼
	•	“Shock-and-kill” or “block-and-lock”: expose latent virus for immune killing or permanently silence provirus respectively
